name: Atazanavir
route_note: oral capsule once daily with food, usually boosted with ritonavir or cobicistat

discovery.note: Azapeptide protease inhibitor with a favourable lipid profile and once-daily dosing. Year of first patent filing (priority April 1996, Ciba-Geigy/Novartis, US 5,849,911).

tagline: Once-daily protease inhibitor known for causing harmless jaundice
summary: Atazanavir is an HIV protease inhibitor that was the first in its class to be taken once daily. It has less effect on blood lipids than older protease inhibitors but frequently raises unconjugated bilirubin, causing jaundice that is usually harmless. Ritonavir-boosted atazanavir has been a WHO-recommended second-line option.
mechanism: Atazanavir binds the active site of HIV-1 protease and prevents cleavage of Gag and Gag-Pol polyproteins, producing immature, non-infectious virions.

It also inhibits the liver enzyme UGT1A1, which conjugates bilirubin; this causes the characteristic indirect hyperbilirubinaemia, particularly in people with Gilbert-type UGT1A1 variants. Its solubility, and therefore absorption, depends on stomach acid.
uses: HIV-1 infection in adults and children (from 3 months in some labels) in combination with other antiretrovirals

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: Reyataz is approved in June 2003 as the first once-daily protease inhibitor; EU approval follows in 2004.

history.title: EU approval
history.detail: Reyataz is approved in the EU in March 2004.

history.title: WHO second line
history.detail: Ritonavir-boosted atazanavir becomes a recommended second-line option in many treatment programmes.

history.title: Evotaz
history.detail: Atazanavir/cobicistat is approved in the US.

history.title: US generics
history.detail: Generic atazanavir capsules are launched in the US.

pk.bioavailability: increased by food; reduced by antacids, H2 blockers and proton-pump inhibitors
pk.metabolism: hepatic CYP3A4; inhibits CYP3A4 and UGT1A1

facts: The jaundice caused by atazanavir reflects unconjugated bilirubin and is not by itself a sign of liver damage.
Proton-pump inhibitors greatly reduce atazanavir absorption and are restricted or avoided.
